slices.text:
Between the two lines the Greeks set one bed, and sang it as comedy. Demodocus' song in the *Odyssey* stages the affair of Ares and Aphrodite from the injured husband's side: Helios — the sun, from whom nothing done on any surface stays hidden — sees the lovers and carries the word to Hephaestus, and the crafter forges his answer, a mesh fine as spider-thread, drapes it over the marriage bed, and springs it on the pair mid-embrace, hauling them up for the assembled gods to inspect (*Odyssey*, VIII.266–366). Every part of the fallen mechanism is present and operating: surveillance, evidence, capture, exposure, the tribunal of laughter — cancellation attempted on the living relation itself. And nothing cancels. The lovers, released, rise and go — she to her sanctuary at Paphos, he to Thrace — undiminished, unashamed, still gods; the only casualty is the marriage of craft, and the laughter, heard again, lands on the net. Alone among these tellings the story carries no death, and the exemption is structural: this is the hinge where the two accountings face each other and the relation reaches neither zero, terminus nor threshold — the fallen line runs its whole apparatus to completion and its sum is nothing, the one result its arithmetic ever promised, while the relation it meant to cancel was never two separable ones at all. From the affair come Harmonia, concord herself, and — Simonides says — Eros (Simonides, fr. 575).

The redeemed line, 2 = 0/1 = 4+2 = 5→0 = 1/0, has its telling too: the myth of Eros and Psyche, which reads as the matheme rendered as a love story. Psyche — the name means soul — is married to a bridegroom she is forbidden to see. The union begins in the dark: the 0/1 held as pure relation, prior to knowledge, prior to the mark. Her sisters work on her; she lights the lamp over the sleeping god — the over-seeing, the grasp that would make the beloved an object — and a drop of hot oil wakes him. Eros flees. The two are thrown apart: the myth contains the dia-ballein inside itself, as the redeemed logic must, since a traversal that never fell would have nothing to return from. Then Psyche labours, and the labours number four. She sorts a mountain of mixed seeds before nightfall, and the ants take pity — the many discerned, grain from grain. She gathers golden fleece from the violent rams of the sun, approaching obliquely at the reed's advice — the radiance taken without being seized. She fills a crystal vessel from the cataract of the Styx, where no mortal foot can stand, by the eagle's flight — the depths drawn without drowning. And fourth, she descends into the underworld itself for a box of Persephone's beauty, and on the way back she opens it — the grasp, once more, at the last step — and falls into a death-sleep, from which Eros himself comes to wake her (Apuleius, _Metamorphoses_, IV.28–VI.24). Four labours: the fourfold work of the made, which the derivation will name the explicate square. And the fourth contains the descent, the death, and the waking — the 5→0 nested where the derivation will place the return. Then the wedding on Olympus, Psyche made immortal; and the child of Soul and Desire is Voluptas — Pleasure, _hēdonē_, ānanda. Bliss is not found in this tale; it is *born* of it, the offspring of a two that laboured, died, and returned. The ending is precise: Eros and Psyche remain two. Married, not merged. Distinction-without-collapse, with the child as proof.

The same shape sings wherever the redeemed line has been told, and always the death is in it: the death is the hinge. Śiva and Pārvatī: her _tapas_, the burning askesis by which she wins the ash-covered renunciate, and their union the engine of the worlds — imaged as the _ardhanārīśvara_, one body half woman and half man, neither dissolved in the other: the symbolon made flesh, distinction-without-collapse rendered so literally you can carve it. The alchemists wed Sol and Luna, King and Queen, and insisted — this is the whole scandal and depth of the art — that the royal pair must first rot: the _nigredo_, the blackening, the two putrefying into the undifferentiated, and only through that death does the Rebis rise, the two-in-one of the _rubedo_ (Jung, CW 12; CW 14). Isis gathers the fourteen scattered pieces of the murdered Osiris and *re-members* him, and from the reassembled body conceives Horus: dismemberment answered by a putting-together that is generative — the re-membering conceives. Inanna descends through seven gates, is stripped of an emblem at each, dies on the hook, and rises; and the land greens. And the taijitu draws the entire doctrine in one curve: yin and yang not as enemies but as two that carry each other's seed, the dot in each eye, flowing round a centre neither owns. In every one of these the death is real — the oil-burn and the exile, the putrefaction, the dismemberment, the hook — and in every one the zero it reaches is a threshold, not a terminus. That is the entire difference between the two lines: two deaths, one minus sign. The devil is the literalist of the minus sign — he reads the zero as cancellation, where the Logos reads it as return.

Plato, in the middle of the _Symposium_, gives the pairing its key almost in passing. Eros, Diotima teaches Socrates, is no god but a great daimon, child of Poros and Penia — Resource and Poverty, fullness and lack — conceived in Aphrodite's garden on the night of her birth; and being born of both, he is constitutionally the between, the _metaxu_, neither having nor lacking but the living traffic between them (_Symposium_, 202d–203e). Eros is not a being that desires. Eros is the desiring-between. The Greeks, who named the diabolon, also drew the slash and gave it a face and a mother and a father — plenty above, poverty below, and the stroke between them prefiguring what the derivation will earn the right to call love.

slices.text:
## 2. The Hephaestus / Ares-Aphrodite / Eros cross-link

This is the piece that ties F1 to the trust-thread and to a linking problem spanning three sections.

**The reading:** Hephaestus's craft-marriage is trust replaced by possession (a made, bounded thing — his own defining trait, applied to a relationship). Ares and Aphrodite's affair is real trust — dangerous, risked, exposed — and it's *generative* (Harmonia; Eros) precisely because it was never bounded. Hephaestus's net is knowledge/surveillance weaponized as a substitute for the trust his marriage never had. And the net fails completely — "nothing cancels" (line 103) — because genuine trust was never the kind of "two" a net can hold. This is not a myth *about* Palantir (line 79); it's the myth Palantir is a footnote to: surveillance cannot manufacture or secure trust, and cannot destroy real trust either — it can only expose the emptiness of a bond that was already false.

**The linking problem Frank flagged:** the early appearance (line 45) needs to presage *two* things downstream, not just the Demodocus payoff — it also needs to properly hand off to Eros, who is the essay's continuous thread from here to nearly the end: Hesiod's primordial Eros (immediately following, same paragraph, line 45), Plato's Symposium's Eros-as-*metaxu* (line 109), the Eros-Psyche myth as the redeemed line's central story (line 105), and "the eros of logos" closing the whole essay (line 267). Eros is not a separate late flourish — it's what's actually born from every instance of this pattern (Ares/Aphrodite's affair; the labour of Psyche), and it is, read through this lens, trust's mythic/desiring face, exactly as syn-ballein/symbolon is trust's structural face.

**Direction:** the line 45 close should do three things in sequence, briefly: (1) name what Hephaestus's marriage lacked and what Ares/Aphrodite's bond had — the trust/possession distinction, using material already present; (2) plant the promissory note that the net's capture will fail to reach what it meant to hold (full payoff deferred to line 103); (3) hand off cleanly to Hesiod's Eros in the very next clause, since Eros is what the affair begets and what will carry this thread through Symposium, Psyche, and the final Epi-Logos section. This turns three currently-loose threads (the net's local point, the Two Deaths payoff, and the Eros throughline) into one deliberate handoff instead of three separate near-misses.

---

F. C. Hull. JSTOR and library catalogues confirm the 1969 Princeton edition, its 699 pages, and its collection of Jung's major shorter writings on religious phenomena. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** C. G. Jung, *Psychology and Religion: West and East*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, *The Collected Works of C. G. Jung*, vol. 11 (Princeton University Press, 1969), {paragraph or page}. **Shortened note:** Jung, *Psychology and Religion*, {paragraph or page}. **Bibliography:** Jung, C. G. *Psychology and Religion: West and East*. Translated by R. F. C. Hull. *The Collected Works of C. G. Jung*, vol. 11. Princeton University Press, 1969. ## Essay use This is the primary Jung carrier for the braid's specific claim that religious images can be treated as psychic realities without being reduced either to external metaphysical objects or to disposable error. It gives the §4 return a proper source distinct from *Aion*, whose work in the corpus remains Self, symbolic totality, and quaternity. **Claim boundary:** the project-held PDF is a locator only and no passage has yet been verified from a lawful selected carrier. This record does not license quotation, establish QL's authorial `X/x`, or collapse Jung's psychology of religion into Freud's metapsychology. ## Passages and excerpts No passage has yet been gathered for this source.

## Apuleius: selected Latin edition recovered; English edition requires checking

The primary [Georgetown Project Libellus full story](https://faculty.georgetown.edu/jod/apuleius/cupid.html) explicitly heads the text APVLEI PSYCHE ET CVPIDO, edited by **Louis C. Purser**, P. H. Lee Warner, Medici Society, London, **1913**, and identifies Metamorphoses IV.28–VI.24. This is an actual recoverable selected Latin edition identity, not an inferred Gaselee edition. The complete story is available in one HTML object; retrieval output was truncated, so this receipt does not claim an unbroken full Latin read.

University-hosted English: [Pomona BookIV](https://pages.pomona.edu/~cmc24747/sources/apuleius/ga_4.htm), [BookV](https://pages.pomona.edu/~cmc24747/sources/apuleius/ga_5.htm), [BookVI](https://pages.pomona.edu/~cmc24747/sources/apuleius/ga_6.htm). These provide the entire narrative; BookVI was read completely through the story ending. They modernize Adlington-like language but do not establish their editor on these pages. Do not cite them as verified Gaselee1915. The Loeb1915 scan retrieval failed; no PDF downloaded.

## Apuleius passage acquisition map and surviving operation

IV.28–35: Psyche's worship displaces Venus, punitive commission, marriage oracle, exposure and Zephyr. V.1–21: unseen household, sisters and staged suspicion. V.22–24: lamp/weapon, self-wound and burning oil, separation. V.25–31: Pan, sisters' deaths and Venus's response. VI.1–9: unsuccessful sanctuary and capture. VI.10: ants sort grain. VI.11–13: reed directs fleece collection. VI.13–15: eagle fetches dangerous water. VI.16–20: tower supplies the descent/return protocol. VI.21: sleep is withdrawn and Cupid rouses Psyche by an arrow point, not a kiss. VI.22–24: divine settlement, immortality, marriage and Voluptas. Exact sentence/chapter allocation must be checked against Purser because the Pomona English puts some23 material under24.

This is a whole supplementary plate: Venus, sisters, helpers, dangerous curiosity, descent and return cannot be reduced to four isolated success tasks. “Marriage without merger” is the project's operation; it is not a phrase or explicit metaphysical doctrine attributed to Apuleius. The tale's narrating old woman/captive listener/Lucius frame must remain recoverable in the eventual full-novel source context.

Proposed Latin house: `submission-package/essay/symbolon/episteme/sources/classical-philology/apuleius/apuleius-1913-psyche-cupido-purser/SOURCE.md`. Candidate cards q001 IV.28–V.24, q002 V.25–VI.9, q003 VI.10–20, q004 VI.21–24. Primary digital Latin identity is ready; full untruncated read and sentence-level quotation collation are still required. English target alternative: Adlington1566 revised Stephen Gaselee1915, The Golden Ass, London Heinemann/New York Putnam, if that actual edition is acquired. Do not promote uncertain Pomona modernization to that work identity. Parent review is required before source creation, as instructed for this bounded task.

Purser. London: P. H. Lee Warner for the Medici Society, 1913. https://faculty.georgetown.edu/jod/apuleius/cupid.html. The title is transcribed from the selected Latin object's heading. Do not substitute Purser's other commentary editions, Gaselee 1915, or an unidentified modernized English text. ## Essay use and narrative integrity The primary tale supplies `mytheme-eros-psyche`, admitted as a supplementary plate at `submission-package/essay/symbolon/mytheme/plates/eros-psyche/WHOLE.md`. It bears the A13/A23 trust relation and A20/A27's image/possession and unity distinction. Its place remains supplementary; this source house does not promote it over the Ares–Aphrodite–Harmonia whole. The project's union-without-merger operation is Argued in its native register. Apuleius is evidence for the tale, not an external proof of that operation. The closing legal possession idiom remains a material friction to be carried, not translated into an assertion that Apuleius himself rejected possession. Four tasks cannot stand for the whole, and a formal four/six relation cannot be established by merely counting them. ## Material metadata and full-read provenance - **Selected object:** Georgetown's Project Libellus text explicitly identifies Purser, Lee Warner, Medici Society, London 1913 in its heading and Richard Clay/Jacobi printing information in its colophon. Full Latin tale covers 4.28–6.24. - **Read coverage:** all 65, 571 normalized text characters, in four contiguous nontruncated reads 0–17000, 17000–34000, 34000–51000, 51000–end, 2026-09-06. Header and colophon included. Raw HTML acquisition hash is recorded in the working acquisition addendum. No full text stored in the canonical house. - **Locator alignment:** [BCS whole-story plan](https://bcs.fltr.ucl.ac.be/apul/amorplan.html) provides chapter/subsection divisions; [6.16.2–21.4](https://bcs.fltr.ucl.ac.be/apul/amor12.html) and [6.22.1–24.4](https://bcs.fltr.ucl.ac.be/apul/amor13.html) checked directly for card alignment. This separately identified French witness supplies navigation, not the selected Latin wording. - **English:** Pomona's complete booksIV–VI offer reading assistance but their modernization's edition is unverified. No English quotation is certified by this Latin house. Named English-edition acquisition remains Open. - **Frame:** the selected excerpt begins 4.28 and ends 6.24. It does not include the old-woman/captive/Lucius framing passages outside those bounds; whole-novel frame quotation remains a separate acquisition task. - **NOTES:** absent; none created. Typographical join/split defects elsewhere in the Libellus text require caution for future long quotations; the short cards below were checked in their local sentences. ## Passages and excerpts ## Passage card — `apuleius-1913-psyche-cupido-purser-q001` — the relation before its exposure Beauty displaces Venus's worship; the oracle sends Psyche to exposure. Zephyr brings her to the unseen household. Her sisters cultivate suspicion; lamp and blade expose Cupid, and burning oil drives separation. - **Locator:**4.28–5.24; revelation 5.21.3–23.5; flight 5.23.6–24.5. - **Status:** paraphrase-ready; no English source quotation. - **Verification:** complete selected Latin read 2026-09-06; chapter route compared with BCS plan. - **Source relation:** paraphrased. - **Evidential action:** supports the whole relational prehistory. - **Consumers:** `mytheme-eros-psyche`; A13; A20; A23. - **Use boundary:** Psyche's action includes attempted violence and bodily curiosity; do not reduce it to a neutral request for evidence. ## Passage card — `apuleius-1913-psyche-cupido-purser-q002` — the helpers and return conditions Pan intervenes; sisters perish; divine sanctuary fails. Venus imposes tasks: ants sort grain, a reed directs fleece collection, an eagle obtains water, and a tower prescribes descent and return. The return needs reserved payments and refusal of deceptive appeals. - **Locator:**5.25–6.20; grain 6.10.1–11.2; fleece 6.11.3–13.1; water 6.13.2–16.1; descent 6.16.2–20.6. - **Status:** paraphrase-ready. - **Verification:** full Latin read 2026-09-06; BCS chapter divisions checked. - **Source relation:** paraphrased. - **Evidential action:** supports whole-task structure; qualifies self-sufficient achievement. - **Consumers:** `mytheme-eros-psyche`; A23; A27. - **Use boundary:** helpers do not prove a generic universal developmental ladder; the native Return obligation needs this particular narrative and its asymmetries. ## Passage card — `apuleius-1913-psyche-cupido-purser-q003` — waking by the arrow > Psychen innoxio punctulo sagittae suae suscitat - **Locator:**6.21.3; whole episode 6.21.1–4. - **Status:** Latin digital quotation-ready; print-image collation Open. - **Verification:** exact seven-word substring transcribed and reread in selected Libellus object 2026-09-06; BCS6.21.3 confirms episode/subsection alignment. - **Source relation:** extracted. - **Evidential action:** corrects a kiss substitution. - **Consumers:** `mytheme-eros-psyche`; A23. - **Use boundary:** after the box releases sleep, Cupid removes it and wakes Psyche with a harmless arrow prick. This is not an English-edition quotation or proof of a psychological mechanism. ## Passage card — `apuleius-1913-psyche-cupido-purser-q004` — union and the legal idiom > sic rite Psyche convenit in manum Cupidinis - **Locator:**6.24.4; settlement 6.22–24; immortality 6.23.5, not 6.24. - **Status:** Latin digital quotation-ready; print-image collation Open. - **Verification:** exact eight-word substring reread 2026-09-06; aligned against BCS6.24.4. Pomona's alternative placement of some material under 24 is not followed. - **Source relation:** extracted; the philosophical operation is argued from the complete tale. - **Evidential action:** supports union while qualifying a false attribution of anti-possession doctrine. - **Consumers:** `mytheme-eros-psyche`; A27; A23. - **Use boundary:** legal marriage, immortality and Voluptas conclude the tale. Its possession language remains visible; a modern juridical claim about Roman marriage requires separate legal evidence. ## Remaining source tasks Inspect a 1913 print image for the short Latin quotations and apparent digital typographical defects if used.
